title: Add artifact lifecycle management from the application UI
objective: Allow authorised users to create new draft artifacts from the library, edit existing artifact metadata and content including adding or removing tags, and safely delete artifacts from the library or editing surface while preserving GitHub as the durable source of truth, optimistic concurrency, production review safeguards, cache correctness, and existing authentication boundaries.
userContext: The user manages artifacts as part of daily work and should not need to open the private storage repository to create a new artifact, maintain its tags, edit draft content, or remove an obsolete artifact. Common lifecycle actions should be available from the application while destructive and production-sensitive changes remain explicit, attributable, conflict-safe, and reviewable.
currentBehaviour: The application has authenticated server-side POST and PATCH APIs and repository primitives for creating and updating artifacts, but it has no general creation or editing UI. The library page provides search and linked artifact cards only. Artifact details provide variation creation and a production-change proposal form. Tags can currently be changed only as part of the production proposal form. There is no repository deletion primitive, deletion API, deletion proposal workflow, or confirmation interface. The generic create and update endpoints accept complete metadata and do not themselves enforce a draft-first creation policy or prevent a caller from invoking a direct production update. The current application specification explicitly excludes brand-new base-artifact creation through the UI and artifact deletion.
requiredBehaviour: Provide an authenticated artifact lifecycle UI. The library must offer creation from scratch. Existing artifacts must have a dedicated editing surface where tags can be added or removed alongside permitted metadata and body changes. Draft and archived artifacts may be updated or deleted through direct, attributable commits using the exact current file SHA. Production updates and production deletions must use reviewable GitHub branches and pull requests and must never directly alter the configured base branch. Every deletion entry point must require explicit confirmation. Server-side policy must enforce these distinctions so direct API calls cannot bypass the production workflow.
userExperience: The library page has a clear Create artifact action. Creating opens a protected editor for a new draft with title, suggested stable ID, type, tags, aliases, and Markdown body. The user can preview and save it, then receives links to the new artifact and GitHub commit. Artifact details provide an Edit action leading to a dedicated editor. Tags are displayed as removable controls and can be added without manually editing YAML or a comma-separated frontmatter string. Draft and archived saves report a direct commit; production saves clearly state that a pull request will be created and that the live artifact remains unchanged. Delete actions are available from each library result and from the editing page. Selecting delete opens an accessible confirmation that identifies the artifact and explains whether confirmation will delete it directly or create a production deletion proposal. Cancelling performs no repository operation. Successful direct deletion removes the artifact from the current list and shows the commit result. A successful production deletion proposal leaves the artifact visible and provides the pull-request link.
functionalRequirements: Add a prominent authenticated Create artifact action to the main library page.
Add a protected creation route, preferably `/artifacts/new`, using the existing shared page chrome, theme behaviour, authentication, and repository-authorisation gate.
Create new base artifacts as `draft` status only through this UI and API workflow. Do not permit the creation form or its endpoint to create an immediately live production artifact.
Collect a required title, stable ID, artifact type, tags, aliases, and non-empty Markdown body.
Suggest a lower-kebab-case ID from the title using the existing slug rules while allowing the user to edit the ID before the first save.
Keep the ID immutable after creation.
Validate the ID, metadata, body, complete serialized UTF-8 size, canonical Markdown, repository path, duplicate global ID, duplicate path, and supported secret patterns before writing.
Provide a private, no-store preview that uses the same Markdown renderer and characterized raw-HTML behaviour as existing artifact previews and performs no repository mutation.
Use the existing authenticated `POST /api/artifacts` write path or a focused extension of it rather than introducing a separate storage implementation.
After successful creation, display only validated local and HTTPS GitHub result links and make the new artifact accessible from the application.
Add a protected artifact editing route, preferably `/artifacts/{id}/edit`, loaded from the same revision-aware artifact snapshot that supplies `currentFileSha`.
Add an Edit action to artifact details.
Use a shared artifact editor where practical so creation, direct editing, and production proposals do not drift into incompatible metadata handling.
Allow title, tags, aliases, and body to be edited.
Display ID, type, source relationship, and creation timestamp as immutable when they are not safely editable.
Do not allow editing to rename or move an existing repository file. Preserve valid existing nested paths.
Represent tags as addable and removable values rather than requiring the user to edit YAML.
Trim tag and alias values, discard empty values, remove exact duplicates while preserving first occurrence order, and retain valid existing casing and ordering unless the user changes them.
Treat status as a policy field rather than a free-text metadata field. Do not permit an ordinary direct update to promote a draft or archived artifact to production.
Allow draft and archived artifacts to be updated directly using the exact file SHA observed with the loaded artifact.
Require production artifact updates, including tag-only changes, to use the existing branch-and-pull-request proposal workflow.

Enforce the production-update restriction on the server and repository boundary. A direct `PATCH /api/artifacts/{id}` request for an existing production artifact must fail with a stable safe error instructing the caller to use the proposal workflow.
Add delete controls to library results and the artifact editing page.
Refactor library card markup so navigation and deletion are separate accessible controls. Do not nest a button inside the existing card Link or rely only on event propagation cancellation.
Require an explicit accessible confirmation before any deletion request or deletion proposal is sent.

The confirmation must display the artifact title and ID, distinguish direct deletion from a production deletion proposal, provide Cancel as a safe default, and prevent duplicate submission while busy.
Cancelling or dismissing confirmation must perform no GitHub, KV, D1, or session mutation.
Obtain or retain the exact current file SHA before deletion. A list deletion may fetch the protected revision-aware artifact endpoint when the card catalogue does not contain the SHA.
Add a typed repository deletion input containing the artifact ID, exact current file SHA, and requesting GitHub login.

For draft and archived artifacts, add a direct deletion method that resolves the current tree, locates the artifact by globally unique ID, validates its existing path, compares its current blob SHA, and issues one GitHub Contents API DELETE request for that exact path and configured base branch.
Use an attributable commit message such as `Delete artifact {id} (requested by @{login})` without artifact content, tags, aliases, credentials, or secrets.
Return a safe direct-deletion result containing the artifact ID, repository-relative path, commit SHA, validated HTTPS commit URL, and repository revision. A deleted file has no new file SHA.
Invalidate the current artifact catalogue pointer after a successful direct deletion using the existing write-completion and invalidation architecture.
Do not turn a successful GitHub deletion into a reported deletion failure merely because cache invalidation is unavailable. Log only the existing safe cache-unavailable category.
Never invalidate the base-branch catalogue merely because a production deletion proposal was opened; the base branch has not changed.
Reject direct deletion of an existing production artifact at the server and repository boundary with a stable `production_delete_requires_proposal` or equivalent typed error.
Add a production deletion proposal workflow that uses the exact base revision, exact existing artifact path, and exact source file SHA.
Create a deterministic bounded branch such as `artifact-delete/{lowercase-artifact-id}-{first-8-file-sha}`.
Represent the proposed file removal through the Git Data tree workflow by deleting the exact tree path rather than replacing the file with empty content.
Use a commit title such as `Propose deletion of artifact {id} (requested by @{login})` and a pull-request title such as `Delete artifact: {title}`.

Keep the deletion pull-request body limited to safe operational metadata: artifact ID, repository-relative path, source file SHA, requesting login, generated-branch attribution, and a statement that Artifact Library will not merge it automatically.
Do not put the artifact body, complete frontmatter, tags, aliases, tokens, cache identifiers, or secrets into the deletion commit message, pull-request body, responses, or logs.
Do not merge, approve, close, or delete the generated branch automatically.

Handle a deterministic branch that already exists without resetting, force-pushing, deleting, or blindly overwriting it. Return an identical open deletion proposal idempotently only after verifying it represents the same deletion; otherwise return a typed branch-collision response.

If the proposal branch is successfully created but pull-request creation fails, return a safe incomplete-proposal response containing only the deterministic branch name and validated GitHub branch URL so the operation can be recovered without repeating unsafe writes.
Use single-attempt mutation semantics for GitHub create, update, delete, branch, commit, and pull-request operations. Do not automatically replay an uncertain mutation.
A stale file SHA must return `409 write_conflict` before any direct DELETE or proposal mutation is sent.
A file removed between preflight and the direct GitHub DELETE must be treated as a conflict or changed state, not silently reported as a successful deletion of the originally observed artifact.
Keep unauthenticated and unauthorised handling ahead of JSON parsing, repository reads, previews, updates, deletes, and proposals.
Use private, no-store responses for all authenticated artifact lifecycle APIs and previews.

Preserve separate safe classifications for validation, secret rejection, oversized content, artifact not found, duplicate ID or path, write conflict, production workflow requirement, authentication, write permission, proposal permission, rate limiting, temporary GitHub failure, malformed GitHub success response, incomplete proposal, and unexpected internal failure.
Unexpected programming errors must continue to reach the generic application boundary rather than being disguised as an empty library, artifact 404, cache miss, or validation error.
Preserve existing GitHub App capability-scoped installation credentials and minimum Metadata read, Contents read/write, and Pull requests read/write permissions.
Preserve DATA-003 cache generation, publication, invalidation, last-known-good, eventual-consistency, and production-binding validation behaviour.
Preserve the existing KV binding and its committed ID exactly. Do not create, remove, replace, or print another namespace ID.

Preserve variation creation, variation preview, production update proposals, catalogue refresh controls, diagnostics, authentication, authorization refresh, theme behaviour, copy behaviour, and deployment identity.
Do not mutate the separate `zailghe3/fpo-artifacts` repository as part of implementing or validating the application feature.

Update the current application specification and relevant README documentation to describe creation, editing, tag management, direct deletion, production deletion proposals, confirmation behaviour, server-enforced production policy, cache effects, and failure states.
technicalConsiderations: Likely new surfaces include a reusable artifact editor, a tag-list editor, an accessible deletion confirmation component, `/artifacts/new`, `/artifacts/[id]/edit`, preview handling, and a focused production-deletion proposal route.

Reuse the existing `prepareWrite`, canonical serializer, size limit, secret scanner, path validation, revision-aware read, safe GitHub URL validation, typed write errors, capability-scoped credentials, and cache invalidation wrapper.
The direct GitHub Contents delete endpoint requires the current file SHA and configured branch and returns commit metadata with null file content.
A Git Data deletion proposal should create a new tree from the exact base tree with the target path deleted, then create one commit, one deterministic branch, and one pull request.
Do not infer deletion paths from the artifact ID. Resolve the valid existing path from the same repository tree used to validate status and SHA so nested paths remain correct.
Do not rely on client-provided status to choose direct deletion versus proposal. Resolve and enforce the current stored status server-side.
Do not trust a client-provided artifact object for authorization, status, path, source relationship, or current revision.
The current generic direct update route can otherwise bypass the production proposal UI; close this policy gap as part of the shared editing implementation rather than relying only on hidden buttons.
Because the library currently wraps each complete card in a Link, list deletion requires a semantic card refactor rather than adding another interactive element inside that Link.
Prefer behavioral Node tests using existing dependencies and exported handlers or pure helpers. Do not add a browser-testing dependency merely for this feature.

Add repository tests for exact-path deletion, nested paths, current-SHA enforcement, stale conflicts, production rejection, permission and service errors, malformed responses, one-attempt mutation behaviour, safe result metadata, deletion proposal creation, branch collision, idempotent proposal recovery, and incomplete pull-request creation.

Add route tests proving authentication and authorization occur before repository operations, direct production update and deletion are rejected, draft creation policy is enforced, responses are private/no-store, and each typed error maps to its intended status and code.

Add UI/helper tests proving tag additions and removals normalize correctly, Cancel performs no deletion request, confirmation is required, safe commit and pull-request links are validated, and list-card markup does not contain nested interactive controls.
Do not replace behavioral tests with assertions that merely search source text.
Do not add dependencies or modify `package-lock.json` unless an unavoidable requirement is first documented. The expected implementation should use the existing stack.

Do not change workflow files, deployment architecture, production secrets, D1 migrations, Cloudflare bindings, or repository permissions beyond documenting that existing Contents and Pull requests write permissions are reused.
outOfScope: Bulk creation, editing, tagging, or deletion.
Tag taxonomy management, tag suggestions, tag colours, tag filtering, or tag analytics.
A recycle bin, soft deletion, scheduled deletion, undelete button, or in-application restoration workflow.
Automatic reversion of a deletion commit.
Automatic merging, approval, branch deletion, or closure of storage-repository pull requests.
Promoting drafts to production or changing the existing production publication policy.
Renaming artifact IDs or moving existing files when type or metadata changes.
Rich-text editing or AI-assisted artifact authoring.
Changing authentication roles or adding multi-user role management.
Modifying the private artifact repository directly during implementation.
Changing KV, D1, Cloudflare Worker, GitHub App, or deployment configuration.
Adding third-party UI, form, modal, validation, or testing dependencies.
acceptanceCriteria: An authorised user can select Create artifact from the main library and create a valid new draft without opening GitHub manually.
The creation form supplies or validates a stable lower-kebab-case ID, required title and body, supported type, tags, and aliases.
Creation preview performs no repository write and uses the shared Markdown rendering behaviour.
Successful creation produces one attributable direct commit, invalidates the catalogue, and displays validated links to the artifact and commit.
The UI and server do not permit the ordinary creation workflow to create an immediately production-status artifact.
Each artifact detail provides an Edit action leading to a protected revision-aware editing surface.
A user can add and remove tags and save the resulting tag array without manually editing frontmatter.
Tag and alias values are trimmed, empty values are removed, and exact duplicates are not persisted.
A draft or archived artifact can be edited directly using its exact current file SHA.
A production artifact edit, including a tag-only edit, creates or returns a reviewable pull request and does not directly alter the base branch.
A direct production PATCH is rejected server-side even when the caller knows a current file SHA.
Delete controls are available from the artifact list and artifact editing page without invalid nested interactive markup.
Every deletion path requires an explicit confirmation, and cancelling performs no repository or cache operation.
A confirmed draft or archived deletion removes the exact existing repository path with the exact current SHA, produces one attributable commit, and invalidates the catalogue.
A confirmed production deletion creates or returns a deterministic deletion pull request and leaves the live base-branch artifact unchanged.
A direct production DELETE request is rejected server-side and cannot bypass the proposal workflow.
Stale update or deletion revisions fail with a safe conflict and issue no write mutation.
Duplicate submissions cannot produce uncontrolled duplicate commits, branches, pull requests, or deletes.
A branch-created/pull-request-failed sequence produces a safe recoverable incomplete-proposal response without leaking artifact content or automatically retrying the mutation.
Authentication, repository authorization, write permission, proposal permission, validation, conflict, not-found, rate-limit, temporary-service, and unexpected failures remain distinguishable.

No token, encrypted token field, session identifier, cookie value, KV key, cache generation, publication identifier, artifact body, complete frontmatter, or raw upstream payload is exposed in responses, logs, confirmation text, commit messages, or pull-request metadata.
Existing variation, proposal, cache, diagnostics, theme, copy, authentication, authorization, and deployment behaviours continue to pass their tests.
No dependency or `package-lock.json` change is introduced.

The complete validation suite passes: clean installation, toolchain validation, tests, lint, typecheck, Next.js build, Worker build, feature-template validation, external-artifact validation, production-binding validation, and whitespace validation.
`specs/000-current-application-spec.md` and relevant user-facing documentation accurately describe the implemented lifecycle behaviour and remove creation and deletion from current exclusions.
The later implementation pull request includes `EDIT-003`, contains an exact `Closes #<generated-issue-number>` reference, and is not merged or deployed automatically by Codex.
codexGuidance: Implement this later from the current main branch after the canonical issue is created. Treat creation, shared editing/tag management, and safe deletion as one lifecycle feature because they reuse the same metadata editor, revision-aware reads, write errors, authorization boundary, result-link validation, and cache rules. Preserve all EDIT-001, EDIT-002, DATA-003, AUTH, OPS diagnostics, and production-binding fixes. Enforce production policy on the server rather than only hiding UI controls. For direct deletion, resolve status, path, and current SHA from one repository tree before sending exactly one Contents API DELETE. For production deletion, reuse the existing proposal architecture but create a deletion tree, deterministic `artifact-delete/...` branch, attributable commit, and non-auto-merged pull request. Do not add unrelated refactors, dependencies, configuration changes, or artifact-repository content.
